title: Mountains and Waters Sutra
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny emphasizes the importance of directly experiencing reality beyond conditioned views and logical thought, encouraging listeners to look beyond their preconceptions and instead embody the paradoxical teachings of the Mountain and Water Sutra, such as "green mountains are always walking" and "eastern mountains travel on water." By embracing these seemingly illogical statements, one can gain a deeper understanding of the Buddha's path and cultivate a sense of freedom from attachment and conditioning. This direct experience allows for a profound connection with nature and the realization of the true dharma wheel of the Tathagata.

sentences.text: Good evening.
We've been looking at Dogen, and I thought to myself, oh, this festival I'm going to be talking about, maybe I'll get into it really deep and do a line by line analysis.
What's he really saying here?
And then I thought, no.
It just became obvious.
At one point I listened to, I think, a six-part lecture, and there were another four full cassette tapes, all on just these few pages, and I thought, well, we've got an hour.
So what are we going to do with an hour?
What we can do is actually look at the sutra.
This is the Mountains and Waters Sutra, Sansuikyo.
For a long time, 17 years now, our sangha has been hiking into the mountains every year to a particular spot, and we have been reciting the sutra during our journey.
I call it sutra walking.
We actually map the sutra over the landscape.
We stop at different places along the way and read a section and then move along.
It takes us a few days to go through our whole journey, to all the different places we're going to go, and at the end we've completed the sutra.
It's called the Mountains and Waters Sutra.
Dogen called it that, although it's obviously not a sutra in the sense that it came from India or even China.
But I'm going to guess that he had some intention in calling it that.
He wanted it to stand alone, in a way, and be considered.
Since it's a very imagistic piece of writing, very evocative, analysis sometimes might do it a bit of a disservice.
And experience, the actual presenting of the sutra, just reading it, reciting it, can do it a better service.
So first, I thought I'd just talk a little bit about how this piece of writing fits into Dogen's life.

I think most of us are pretty aware of the general outline of Dogen's life: he was a young monk, became a monk at the age of 13, and after many years of study in Japan under two of the predominant schools, different schools, he just remained dissatisfied and took a trip to Japan for several years, where he basically found what he was looking for and came back.
Upon coming back, he essentially created a reform movement in Japan.
So I think it's good to have a little bit of a sense of where that history of his life fits into the Japan that he lived in.
Kaz Tanahashi and many others translated the entire Shobujenzo, and in this more recent edition from just a couple years ago, Kaz writes something very succinct about that.
It's as easy as anything to just read it.
*In Japanese history, the era when Dogen lived is called the Kamakura period.
That's 1185 to 1333.
Before that, the preceding periods were the Asuka period, 593 to 710.
And after that, the Nara period, 710 to 794.
After that, the Heian period, 794 to 1185.
And then that brings us up to the Kamakura period, which is where Dogen lived.
So Buddhist doctrine was introduced to Japan through Chinese language texts from Korea in the mid-sixth century.
And since Buddhism was accompanied by the writing system and advanced technology of a great civilization, it quickly received imperial patronage and spread throughout the country.
The appointment of Prince Shotoku as a regent, who was to dedicate his life to the practice and propagation of Buddhism, marked the beginning of the Asuka period.*
*The grid-shaped city planning of Nara, the new capital of Japan, followed that of the Chinese capital city of Chang'an.

The construction of the Todai temple, which housed an enormous Buddha statue, exemplified a concerted national effort initiated by the monarch to create a society based on the infinite luminosity of the universal Buddha light described in the Avatamsaka Sutra.
The six schools of Buddhism, most of which were based on various philosophical principles, flourished.*
So that was basically the events of the first couple periods, several hundred years of Buddhism in Japan.
*The larger scale planned city of Heian, Kyoto, to the north of Nara, became the imperial capital where highly refined court culture developed.
Trade with China increased, number of monks studied in Tang, China, a flourishing world empire.
The Shingon Mantra school, focused on highly ritualized esoteric Buddhist prayers, became one of the two most influential schools of Buddhism in Japan.
The Tendai school, the Japanese form of the Tiantai school in China, was the other powerful school with a comprehensive Buddhist training center on Mount Hiei in the northeast of Kyoto.
Assimilating with the indigenous Shintoism, Buddhism became an indispensable part of everyday life.
Buddhist masters competed with one another to gain imperial patronage, offering a variety of magical prayers.
Mount Hiei housed one of the strongest armies of monk soldiers who frequently engaged in battles, sometimes burning other monasteries.*
*The Tendai armed forces were known for their frequent demonstrations in Kyoto and for forcing their demands upon the imperial government.
According to Buddhist texts, the period of 500 years after the time of Shakyamuni Buddha is the age of true Dharma, which is followed by another 500 years of the age of imitation Dharma.
Then the age of declining Dharma emerges.
Many Japanese Buddhists believed that this last period of declining Dharma of no true practice or enlightenment started in 1052.
People attributed calamities such as famines, epidemics, social disorder, and wars to the decline of Dharma.
The wish to attain rebirth in the pure land prevailed among those who felt that it was hopeless to attain enlightenment in the present world.*
*The samurai families, the Taira clan from the western part of the country and the Minamoto from the east served as imperial guards and expanded their influence.
First, Kiyomura Taira became a powerful military ruler, still serving the emperor.
Then Yoritoma Minamoto defeated the Taira armies in a series of battles and established the Shogun government in Kamakura.
This was the beginning of the Kamakura period.*

So the Kamakura period that Dogen lived in was a period of famine, war, wandering, itinerant samurai, and generally thought of as being a time of really declined Buddhist practice, corrupted, fully entrenched with government and power.
*Buddhism in this period may be characterized by the emergence of single practice.

Honen and his noted disciple Shinran came into conflict, a conflict with the Tendai establishment which forced them into exile, but they succeeded in spreading the wholehearted practice of chanting homage to Amitabha Buddha.
Dogen established the Zen practice of just sitting, Shikantaza, and later Nitren spread the practice of chanting homage to the Lotus Sutra, Namo Mio Rengekyo.
This single practice of Buddhism in all its variations appealed to great numbers of farmers, warriors, court nobles, and eventually became the mainstream of faith in Japan.*
So it's interesting, I think, to get a sense of what Dogen was dealing with, especially when you see in his writings how he was reacting against this time period.
When he first set up his teaching, the very first text he wrote was Phukan Zazengi, which is in our chant book, recommending Zazen to all people.

It was his declaration of a single practice available to everyone, and that was followed a few years later by him writing Bendawa, on the Endeavor of the Way, and a series of other writings such as Genjokoan.
These were some of the earliest writings in his big compendium of Shobujenzo.
In 1240, which was 13 years into his teaching, he really started hitting a stride in writing.

Many fascicles were written in that year, beginning with, well, there were just many, but at one point one of the fascicles was given as a letter or gift to a student of the time being, Uji, and that was followed on the same day by his presentation of the Power of the Robe, the Transmission of the Robe, as a talk.
About two weeks later, he brought the assembly together at midnight for a Dharma talk, the Hour of the Rat, and he presented the Mountains and Waters Sutra.
Kaz here says that Dogen gave only 31 formal talks, as opposed to informal talks or whatever, but very formal talks, between 1235 and 1240, a five-year period.
So it wasn't a very common thing for him to give a formal talk like this, and he did it at midnight.

That gets you a little bit up to date with how this piece of writing fits into his work as a teacher and the community of students he'd gotten together at that point, and what he was trying to present, just very briefly, without too much analysis about what he was teaching at that point.
But what I'd like to do right now is hand out the sutra, everybody can get a copy.
Give me one, oh no, I've got this one here, that's good, right.
So what we're all going to do is pretend that we're on the mountains, and in this backpack, okay.

First we meet, we form a group, we have all our gear, we have to figure out what we're doing, we have to figure out how we're going to reduce our lives down for a few days into the bare essentials, the things we can actually carry.
That's a processing in itself.
To become a group that steps into the wilderness, you're automatically a group, as if you were starting a Zen retreat, just automatically without really adding anything to what's happening.
Already you have a container, and to heighten the sense of entering that container, we do a Native American sweat lodge next door the night before we take off.
I have a friend who's trained in this, and we've been doing this now for many, many years.
We do a sort of Zen sweat lodge.
If you haven't ever done this before, I'll explain it briefly.
It's essentially a purification ceremony of rebirth.
That's why traditionally you take off all your clothes and you're just naked like a baby.
You go into this dark, womb-like place that's really hot, and there's ceremony and prayers and chanting, and the door is opened four times.
It's done in four rounds, which is symbolic of four stages of life or four stages of understanding.
After you're done with the sweat lodge, you feel like you're done with the sweat lodge.
You're really ready for the next thing, and that's perfect, because you're ready for the next thing.
We take off for the mountains really early the next morning, after having stated something in the sweat lodge about what our intention is.
What are we bringing to this?
Now, where we go is our mountain.

This ritual that we do is part of a whole series of rituals that sets us in place and honors and recognizes this place where we are living in its natural reality, in other words, most directly in its watershed consciousness.
Throughout the season, we do a series of hikes where we start low and we head up the watershed to the high country, and then we travel back.
This would be our highest high country trip of this watershed area, of this series of trips.
Any one of these trips that we do is part of a whole larger arc of rituals, and reciting the Mountains and Waters Sutra then becomes really penultimate of that entire cycle of rituals.
We go to a trail, the same trail, and we walk the same path that we've always walked.
It's an out-and-back, a pilgrimage route essentially, in that sense.
The places we stop are the same places each time.
We drive all the way down to Skagit and up the west side of Baker Lake, and we head up like we're heading towards Mount Baker, towards Shriver's Meadows, which is a very popular hike.
But then we turn off, we don't head that way, and we head around all the way behind the Twin Sisters to our trailhead.
It's called Pioneer Horse Camp on the map.
It's seven and a half miles and 1500 foot elevation gain that we try and do in one day.
We do this hiking in silence.
We enter the woods like it's the Zendo.
We have our packs.
We hit the clackers.
We bow.
We head up the trail.
We have a person at the front of the line, a person at the back of the line, and that way we stay together.
We have some rules so that we can do what we do and stay safe while not really having to talk.
The trail crosses the upper reaches of the South Fork and the Nooksack on a bridge.
Then we cross a couple other tributary streams and we're traveling through old growth hemlock forest with a very wide open kind of understory.
We reach a place where there are a few long switchbacks that come up, and we come to a high bench of land in the big forest, large trees.
There are some downed logs there.
We set our packs.
There's a very large tree that on the side of it has had a lightning strike.
You can see the spiral mark, a groove in the trunk that was made long ago when the lightning hit it and traveled to the ground.
We set up a candle and the incense there.
We pull out our sutras.
We pull out our rakasus out of our packs.
We have a bell, and we begin our rituals.
So this is where we're at now.
We can imagine we're there, and we're all going to begin by reciting the Mountains and Waters Sutra.

One thing before we start that's going to be interesting, especially for those who have actually done the trip before, is that the version that we're reading here tonight is different than the one we've read for so many years.
It's a more recent revision.
It'll be interesting because it makes it fresh for us.
There are changes in here, and I might end up pointing out some of those as we go along.
We'll recite altogether out loud just like we're in a service, and at some point I'll tell us, okay, this is the point.
So, Mountains and Waters Sutra.
*Mountains and Waters Sutra.
Mountains and waters right now actualize the ancient Buddha expression.
Each abiding in its condition unfolds its full potential.
Because mountains and waters have been active since before the empty eon, they are alive in this moment.
Before form arose, they are emancipation.
Because the mountains are high and broad, their way of riding the clouds always extends from the mountains.
Their wondrous power soaring in the wind comes freely from the mountains.*
*Priest Dautai of Mount Furong said to the assembly, the green mountains are always walking.
A stone woman gives birth to a child at night.
Mountains do not lack the characteristics of mountains.
Therefore, they always abide in ease and always walk.
Examine in detail the characteristics of the mountains walking.
Mountains walking is just like human walking.
Accordingly, do not doubt mountains walking even though it does not look the same as human walking.
The Buddha ancestor's words point to walking.
This is fundamental understanding.
Penetrate these words.
Because green mountains walk, they are permanent.
Although they walk more swiftly than the wind, someone in the mountains does not notice or understand it.*
*In the mountains means the blossoming of the entire world.
People outside the mountains do not notice or understand the mountains walking.
Those with eyes to see mountains cannot notice, understand, see, or hear this reality.
If you doubt mountains walking, you do not know your own walking.
It is not that you do not walk, but that you do not know or understand your own walking.
Since you do know your own walking, you should fully know the green mountains walking.
Green mountains are neither sentient nor insentient.
You are neither sentient nor insentient.
At this moment, you cannot doubt the green mountains walking.
You may not notice*
*that you study the green mountains using numerous worlds of phenomenon as your standards.
Clearly examine the green mountains walking and your own walking.
Examine walking backward and backward walking.
Investigate the fact that walking forward and backward has never stopped since the very moment before form arose, since the time of the ending of the empty eon.
If walking had stopped, buddha ancestors would not have appeared.
If walking ends, the buddha dharma cannot reach the present.
Walking forward does not cease.
Walking backward does not cease.
Walking forward does not obstruct walking backward.
Walking backward does not obstruct walking forward.
This is called the mountains flow and the flowing mountains.*
*Green mountains thoroughly practice walking and eastern mountains thoroughly practice traveling on water.
Accordingly, these activities are a mountain's practice.
Keeping its own form without changing body and mind, a mountain always practices in every place.
Don't slander by saying that a green mountain cannot walk and an eastern mountain cannot travel on water.
When your understanding is shallow, you doubt the phrase "green mountains are always walking."
When your learning is immature, you are shocked by the words "flowing mountains."
Without fully understanding even the words "flowing water," you drown in small views and narrow understanding.
Yet the characteristics of mountains manifest their form and life force.*
*There is walking, there is flowing, and there is a moment when a mountain gives birth to a mountain child.
Because mountains are buddha ancestors, buddha ancestors appear in this way.
Even if you have an eye to see mountains as grass, trees, earth, rocks, or walls, do not be confused or swayed by it.
This is not complete realization.
Even if there is a moment when you view mountains as the seven treasures' splendor, this is not returning to the source.
Even if you understand mountains as the realm where all buddhas practice, this understanding is not something to be attached to.
Even if you have the highest understanding of mountains as all buddhas' wondrous characteristics, this truth is not only this.
These are conditioned views.*
*This is not the understanding of buddha ancestors, but merely looking through a bamboo pipe at a corner of the sky.
Turning circumstances and turning the mind is rejected by the great sage.
Speaking of mind and speaking of essence is not agreeable to buddha ancestors.
Seeing into mind and seeing into essence is the activity of people outside the way.
Confined words and faces do not lead to liberation.
There is something free from all these views.
That is, green mountains are always walking and eastern mountains travel on water.
Study this in detail.*

We put them in our packs.
We raise our packs again.
Then the clackers come together.
We bow and we head down the trail.
Shortly after that we come to the stream, again the upper fork of the south fork.
We stop to have lunch.
Meal chant.
We eat in silence.
We don't take too long.
We cross the stream.
We reach a trail junction, take a right, head around the toe of the ridge, and we begin a long, slow traverse upwards through the woods, heading towards the ridge line.
We're walking silently and we're thinking about these words.
We're wondering, "Well, this didn't really leave me too much room to move, did it?
Everything was sort of eliminated from consideration."
All these conditioned views, looking through a bamboo tube at a corner of the sky.
You wonder, what am I doing?
What is the mountains flowing?
Are green mountains walking?
Dogen says, don't doubt mountains walking.
Since you do know your own walking, you should fully know the green mountains walking.
You get to work with that every step.
It's a really wonderful practice.
One time we're heading up that long traverse.
We're deep into this practice, silent.
And off to the right, the steep side slope heading down, off to the right, down slope, 100 feet, but up in the trees, almost at our eye level, we hear this big whoosh.
We all turn just in time to see a whole top of a tree, maybe 50 feet long, that was caught up in these trees.
It had split off at some time before and was caught up in these trees.
At that moment, it gave way and fell 60 or 70 feet down.
We all turned, kept walking.
It was really a deep moment.
We reach up the pass, Bell Pass, this beautiful, very shallow pond there with lots of dragonflies.
It's a place to rest with some logs to put your pack on.
There's been a steep section getting there, so we take a little break.
And we move along.
Now we go over the ridge line, and now we're actually in the middle fork drainage.
So we've come into another drainage of the three tributaries of our watershed.
And we sort of take a right and we're heading up this ridge line now.
Occasionally we're starting to actually get glimpses of the mountain.
And then at some point we come to a place where the trees part, and we're looking up and there's the Black Buttes and the summits of Baker rising up out of the forest, floating up there.

As we come around a little corner in the trail, we suddenly come upon a little declivity where a stream coming from higher ground, a little perennial stream, comes and tumbles over these beautiful sets of rocks in a rivulet and splashes on these pools, this little pool right there, and these rough rocks.
And we take our packs off again.
And we pull out our sutras and we set up the candle.
And we begin the next section of the sutra.
We always start Mountains and Waters Sutra:
*A stone woman gives birth to a child at night means that the mountain, when a barren woman gives birth to a child, is called night.
They are male stones, female stones, and non-male, non-female stones placed in the sky and in the earth.
They are called heavenly stones and earthly stones.
These are explained in the ordinary world, but not many people know about it.
Understand the meaning of "gives birth to a child."
At the moment of giving birth to a child, is the mother separate from the child?
Study not only that you become a mother when your child is born, but also that you become a child.
This is to actualize giving birth in practice realization.
Study and investigate this thoroughly.*
*Yuen Men, great master, Kwan Zen said, "Eastern mountains travel on water."
The meaning of these words is that all mountains are eastern mountains and all eastern mountains travel on water.
Because of this, nine mountains, Mount Samaro, and other mountains appear and have practice realization.
These are called eastern mountains.
However, could Yuen Men penetrate the skin, flesh, bones, and marrow of the eastern mountains and their vital practice realization?*
*Now in Great Song China, there are careless fellows who form groups.
They cannot be set straight by the few true masters.
They say that the statement "eastern mountains travel on water" or Nanquan's story of a sickle is illogical.
What they mean is that any words having to do with logical thought are not buddha ancestors' Zen words and that only illogical stories are buddha ancestors' expressions.
In this way, they consider Huang Bo striking with a staff and Lin Ji's shout as beyond logic and unconcerned with thought.
They regard these as words of great enlightenment that precede the arising of form.
They say ancient masters use expedient phrases which are beyond understanding to slash entangled vines.
Those who say this have never seen a true master and they have no eye of understanding.
They are immature, foolish fellows not even worth discussing.*
*In China, these two or 300 years, there have been many groups of demons and six types of heretical thinkers.
What a pity.
The great road of buddha ancestors is crumbling.
People who hold this view are not even as good as shravakas of the lesser vehicles and are more foolish than those outside the way.
They are neither lay people nor monks, neither human nor heavenly beings.
They are more stupid than animals that learn the buddha way.
The illogical stories mentioned by those bald-headed fellows are only illogical for them, not for great ancestors.
Even though they do not understand, they should not neglect studying the buddha ancestors' path of understanding.
Even if it is beyond understanding in the end, their present understanding is off the mark.*
*I have personally seen and heard many people like this in Song China.
How sad that they do not know about the phrases of logical thought or penetrating logical thought in phrases.
When I laughed at them in China, they had no response and remained silent.
Their idea about illogical words is only a distorted view.
Even if there is no teacher to show them the original truth, their belief in spontaneous enlightenment is a view of those outside the way.
Know that "eastern mountains travel on water" is the marrow of the buddha ancestors.
All waters appear at the foot of the eastern mountains.
Accordingly, all mountains ride on clouds and walk in the sky.*
*All mountains are the tops of the heads of all waters.
Walking beyond and walking within are both done on water.
All mountains walk with their toes on waters and make them splash.
Thus, in walking there are seven paths and eight horizontal paths.
This is practice realization.
Water is neither strong nor weak, neither light nor dry, neither moving or still, neither cold nor hot, neither existent nor non-existent, neither diluted nor enlightened.
When water solidifies, it is harder than a diamond.
Who can crack it?
When water melts, it is softer than milk.
Who can destroy it?
Do not doubt that these are the characteristics water manifests.
Reflect on the moment when you see water of the ten directions as water of the ten directions.
This is not merely studying the moment when human and heavenly beings see water.
This is studying the moment when water sees water.
Because water practices and realizes water, water expresses water.
Actualize the path where self encounters self.
Go forward and backward, leaping beyond the final path where other fathoms other.*

Sometimes it's raining.
It's raining in the mountains.
It's a big deal because you don't want to get wet, too wet.

So we make it to camp.
There's a little steep section there.
We're usually kind of tired.
We usually get there later than we want.
And there's this beautiful little log hut up there.
And we've got some tarps and stuff bungeeing in the rafters.

We get the rock.

Little place for a candle.
And we have an evening zazen schedule and a morning zazen schedule.

The next morning we do a little solo excursion out in the meadows.
People get set out for a few hours to be with their place.
And we do that like dokusan.
We start in zazen and then somebody says come to dokusan, so people get taken and they get put out there and then they come back.
We come back a few hours later and we're back in zazen.
In the afternoon of that next day we break silence and we say, you know, let's just have fun.
We're in the mountains.
So we go for a day hike and we head up and there's this beautiful fire lookout a thousand feet above us at the top of Park Butte.
It's not that hard to get to.
It's classic.

Of course this part of the world has this great tradition of some zen crazies heading up into the mountains to find their version of being a zen hermit, which in this world around here is being a fire lookout.
My dad was a fire lookout maybe three or four years before Kerouac and Snyder, Dad in Oregon, 1948, 1949, Odell Butte.

I think this is like a G4.
It's a particular kind of floor plan.
So if you ever get a chance to go up there, it's very well maintained and it's first come, first served.
You can stay there tonight.
It's maintained by a local hiking group.
So the next day after morning practice we pack it up and we take the whole zendo apart and pack it together, and we take the big rock and we take it back out into the meadow and we place it.
So now we're facing the mountain and we pull out our sutras again.
Mountains and Waters Sutra:
*Not all beings see mountains and waters in the same way.
Some beings see water as the jeweled ornament, but they do not regard jeweled ornaments as water.
What in the human realm corresponds to their water?
We only see their jeweled ornaments as water.
Some beings see water as wondrous blossoms, but they do not use blossoms as water.
Hungry ghosts see water as raging fire or pus and blood.
Dragons and fish see water as a palace or a pavilion.
Some beings see water as the seven treasures or a wish-granting jewel.
Some beings see water as a forest or a wall.
Some see it as the Dharma nature of pure liberation, the true human body, or the form of the body and the essence of mind.
Human beings see water as water.
Water is seen as dead or alive depending on the seer's causes and conditions.
Thus the views of all beings are not quite the same.
You should question this matter now.
Are there many ways to see one thing, or is it a mistake to see many forms as one thing?
Pursuit is beyond the limit of pursuit.
Accordingly, endeavors in practice realization of the way are not limited to one or two kinds.
The thoroughly actualized realm has 1,000 kinds in 10,000 ways.*
*When we think about the meaning of this, it seems that there is water for various beings but there is no original water.
There is no water common to all types of beings.
But water for these various kinds of beings does not depend on mind or body, does not arise from actions, does not depend on self or other.
Water's freedom depends only on water.
In this way water is not just earth, water, fire, wind, space or consciousness.
Water is not blue, yellow, red, white or black.
Water is not form, sound, smell, taste, touch or mind.
But water as earth, water, fire, wind and space actualizes itself.
This being so*
*It is difficult to say who has created this land and palace right now or how such things have been created.
To say that the world is resting on the wheel of space or on the wheel of wind is not the truth of the self or the truth of others.
Such a statement is based only on a small view of assumptions.
People speak this way because they think that it's impossible for things to exist without having a place to rest.
The Buddha said all things are ultimately unbound.
There is nowhere that they permanently abide.
Know that even though all things are unbound and not tied to anything they abide in their own condition.
However when most human beings see water they only see that it flows unceasingly.
This is a limited human view.*
*There are actually many kinds of flowing.
Water flows on the earth, in the sky, upwards and downwards.
It flows around a single curve or into many bottomless abysses.
When it rises it becomes clouds.
When it descends it forms abysses.
Wenzi said the path of water is such that when it rises to the sky it becomes raindrops.
When it falls to the ground it becomes rivers.
Even a secular person can speak this way.
You who call yourselves descendants of Buddha ancestors should feel ashamed of being more ignorant than an ordinary person.
The path of water is not noticed by water but is actualized by water.
It is not unnoticed by water but is actualized by water.
When it rises to the sky it becomes raindrops.*
*Means that water rises to the heavens and skies and forms raindrops.
Raindrops vary according to the different worlds.
To say that there are places water does not reach is the teaching of the shravakas of the lesser vehicles or the mistaken teaching of people outside the way.
Water exists inside fire and inside mind, thought and discernment.
Water also reaches inside realization of Buddha nature.
When it falls to the ground it becomes rivers.
Means that when water reaches the ground it turns into rivers.
The essence of the rivers becomes a wise person.
Ordinary fools and mediocre people nowadays think that water is always in rivers or oceans but this is not so.
There are rivers and oceans within water.*
*Thus even where there is not a river or an ocean there is water.
It is just that when water falls down to the ground it manifests the characteristics of rivers and oceans.
Also do not think that where water forms rivers or oceans there is no world and there is no buddha land.
Even in a drop of water innumerable buddha lands appear.
Accordingly it is not that there is only water in the buddha land or a buddha land in water.
Where water abides is not concerned with the past, future, present or the worlds of phenomenon.
Yet water is the fundamental point actualized.
Where buddha ancestors reach, water never fails to reach.
Where water reaches, buddha ancestors never fail to be present.*
*Thus buddha ancestors always take up water and make it their body and mind.
Make it their thoughts.*
We recite this while looking at the mountain, at the huge glaciers hanging there, the sources of all the watersheds, of all the waters in this area, coming down from there.
For time immemorial people have traveled to mountains, and part of that traveling is to honor this cycle of water: its endlessness and its source and its different types of manifestations.
Dogen is certainly talking about this.
What is water, and how is it important to all different beings?

We head down the trail hoisting our packs, we say goodbye to camp, and it doesn't take us too long and we come around a corner and there is a dry valley, a rocky valley, looking directly down the long South Fork, Middle Fork valley.
It's a beautiful sort of interior valley view, and we pull out our sutras again, Mountains and Waters Sutra.
*In this way the words "water does not rise" are not found in scriptures inside or outside of buddha dharma.
The path of water runs upward, downward and in all directions.
Buddha said to us, say fire and air go upward, earth and water run downward.
This upward and downward require examination.
Examine this from the point of view of the buddha way.
Although you use the word downward to describe the direction earth and water go, earth and water do not actually go downward in the same way the directions fire and air go.
The world of phenomenon is not limited by up, down or the cardinal directions.
They are tentatively designated according to the directions in which four great elements, five great elements, six great elements go.
The heaven of no thought should not be regarded as upward, nor should the hell be regarded as downward.
The Avici hell is the entire world of phenomenon.
The heaven of no thought is the entire world of phenomenon.*
*Now when dragons and fish see water as a palace, it may be like human beings seeing a palace.
They may not think it flows.
If an outsider tells them, "What you see is a palace, it is running water," the dragons and fish may be astonished, just as we are when we hear the words "mountains flow."
Nevertheless there may be some dragons and fish who understand that the railings and pillars and palaces and pavilions are flowing water.
Quietly reflect and ponder the meaning of this.
If you do not learn to penetrate your superficial views you will not be freed from the body and mind of an ordinary person.
Then you will not thoroughly experience the land of buddha ancestors or even the land or the palace of ordinary people.*
*At this time human beings deeply know that what is in the ocean and the river is water, but do not know what dragons and fish see and use as water.
Do not foolishly suppose that what we see as water is used as water by all other beings.
You who study with buddhas should not be limited to human views when you see water.
Go further and study water in the buddha way.
Study how you view the water used by buddha ancestors.
Study whether there is water or no water in the home of buddha ancestors.*
*Mountains have been the abode of great sages from the limitless past to the limitless present.
Wise people and sages all have mountains as their inner chambers, as their body and mind.
Because of wise people and sages mountains are actualized.
You may think that in mountains many wise people and great sages are assembled, but after entering the mountains not a single person meets another.
There is just the vital activity of the mountains.
There is no trace of anyone having entered the mountains.
When you see the mountains from the ordinary world and when you meet mountains while in mountains, the mountains' head and eye are viewed quite differently.*
*Your idea or view of mountains not flowing is not the same as the view of dragons and fish.
Human and heavenly beings have attained a position concerning their own worlds that other beings may doubt or may not have the capacity to doubt.
Do not remain bewildered and skeptical when you hear the words "mountains flow," but study these words with buddha ancestors.
When you take up one view you see mountains flowing.
When you take up another view, mountains are not flowing.
Another time they are not flowing.
If you do not fully understand this, you do not understand the true dharma wheel of the Tathagata.
An ancient buddha said, if you do not wish to incur the cause for unceasing hell, do not slander the true dharma wheel of the Tathagata.
Are these words on your skin, flesh, bones and marrow, on your body, mind and environs, on emptiness and on form?
They are already carved on trees and rocks, on fields and villages.*
There's some poignancy: we're leaving the mountains at this point.
We're heading down, and we've pretty thoroughly turned ourselves around.
We're heading out the path we came, but things look different.
Things always look different the other way around, right?
We notice things we didn't notice before.
We look at maps, we try and figure our way, we try and keep our direction going right.
But Dogen's telling us that up is down and down is up, and what we think is the right direction is actually the opposite direction.
But then he says:
*You may think that in mountains many wise people and great sages are assembled, but after entering the mountains not a single person meets another.
There's just the vital activity of the mountains.
There's no trace of anyone having entered the mountains.*
Which of course is what we want.
We don't want to leave a trace.
We're just passing through, but we're feeling the vital activity of the mountains.
So we head on down.

We have our lunch at Bell Pass this time, and we continue on down the trail, across the South Fork again at our old lunch spot, and as we come up to a rise, as we're coming off the creek, we come to a high point where we can see the back side of the Twin Sisters and a beautiful view to the south.
There's a rock outcropping and we set up our candle there for the final time.

We begin with what must have been a bit of a statement Dogen was making, because some years after this, of course, he took his monastic community away from the outskirts of Kyoto and up to the mountains and created Eiheiji, partly because it was a place he could practice more disturbed from the political pressures of the time.
So we pick up our sutras again, we light the candle, Mountains and Waters Sutra.
*Although mountains belong to the nation, mountains belong to people who love them.

When mountains love their master, such a virtuous sage or wise person enters the mountains, and since mountains belong to the sages and wise people living there, trees and rocks become abundant and birds and animals are inspired.
This is so because the sages and wise people extend their virtue.
Know for a fact that mountains are fond of wise people and sages.
Rulers pay homage to wise people, would ask instruction from great sages.
These has been excellent precedences in the past and present.
At such times these rulers treat the sages as teachers, disregarding the protocol of the usual world.
The imperial power has no authority over the wise people in the mountains.
Mountains are apart from the human world.
At the time the Yellow Emperor visited Mount Kongtong to pay homage to Guangcheng, he walked on his knees, touching his forehead to the ground, and asked for instruction.*
*When Shakyamuni Buddha left his father's palace and entered the mountains, his father the king did not resent the mountains, nor was he suspicious of those who taught the prince in the mountains.
The twelve years of Shakyamuni Buddha's practice of the way were mostly spent in the mountains, and his opening of the way occurred in the mountains.
Thus even his father, a wheel turning king, did not wield authority in the mountains.
Know that mountains are not the realm of human beings or the realm of heavenly beings.
Do not view mountains from the standard of human thought.
If you do not judge mountains flowing by the human understanding of flowing, you will not doubt mountains flowing and not flowing.*
*On the other hand, from ancient times wise people and sages have often lived on water.
When they live on water they catch fish, catch human beings and catch the way.
These are all ancient ways of being on water.
Following wind and streams, furthermore, there is catching the self, catching catching, being caught by catching and being caught by the way.
Priest Decheng abruptly left Mount Yao and lived on the river.
There he produced a successor, the wise sage of the Huating river.
Is this not catching a fish, catching a person, catching water or catching the self?
The disciples seeing that Decheng is Decheng.
Decheng guiding his disciple is meeting a true person.*
*It is not only that there is water in the world but there is a world in water.
It is not merely in water.
There is a world of sentient beings in clouds.
There is a world of sentient beings in the air.
There is a world of sentient beings in fire.
There is a world of sentient beings on earth.
There is a world of sentient beings in the world of phenomenon.
There is a world of sentient beings in a blade of grass.
There is a world of sentient beings in one staff.
Wherever there is a world of sentient beings, there is a world of Buddha ancestors.
Thoroughly examine the meaning of this.
In this way, water is the true dragon's palace.
It is not flowing downward.*
*To regard water as only flowing is to slander water with the word flowing.
This would be the same as insisting that water does not flow.
Water is just the true thusness of water.
Water is water's complete characteristics.
It is not flowing.
When you investigate the flowing and not flowing of a handful of water, thorough experience of all things is immediately actualized.

There are mountains hidden in treasures, there are mountains hidden in swamps, there are mountains hidden in the sky, there are mountains hidden in mountains, there are mountains hidden in hiddenness.
This is how we study.*
*An ancient Buddha said, mountains are mountains, waters are waters.
These words do not mean mountains are mountains, they mean mountains are mountains.
In this way, investigate mountains thoroughly.
When you investigate mountains thoroughly, this becomes the endeavor within the mountains.
Such mountains and waters of themselves become wise persons and sages.*
So the sages and wise people extend their virtue in the mountains.
And we've traveled through the mountains.
We've seen how the world of sentient beings exists everywhere.

So we walk through the woods, we find spider webs we can't see, we encounter the pollen dust, we see the tiny little hemlock seedlings scattered on the ground at the feet of the immense, huge ancient hemlocks.
We see the great depth, the innumerable depth, of sentient beings everywhere.
And we wonder, how do we penetrate all this?
And Dogen says, mountains are not mountains, mountains are mountains.
Well, they say when you first come to practice, you see things just as ordinary things, the way you've sort of always seen them.
Then when you get into practice, at some point, you see things completely taken apart, not as themselves anymore, as empty, as particle, form, all, no boundary, no distinction.
But eventually you really see that things exist in their own conditions, just as we do, and that they fully embody those conditions, like a mountain does.
And that's what Dogen's talking about.
He says that that's hidden, like it's in plain sight.
It's hidden in hiddenness.
It's almost at the end of your nose.
But eventually you see it.
We finish, and we recite a dedication.
When we do these services, we always have a dedication.
We have a special dedication that we use in the mountains.
Let's call it gratitude to nature.
We say:
*We've offered candles and incense, and we've chanted the Mountains and Waters Sutra.
Whatever merit comes to us from these offerings, we now return to the earth, sea, and sky, and dedicate our gratitude to nature.

Remembering the stillness, the clarity, the kindness that is the true nature of all life, remembering the way of life day by day that accords with Buddha, and remembering the community of all beings that is our inspiration and support.
May the air be left pure.
May the waters be clean.
May the earth be restored.
May we attain Buddha's way together with all beings.*
And we chant, as we always do:
*All Buddhas, ten directions, three times.
All Buddhas, ten directions, three times.*

The grid-shaped city planning of Nara, the new capital of Japan, followed that of the Chinese capital city of Chonan.
